title: Pay No Heed to the Slanderers, What They Said and What They Passed On
intro: A poem of love and wisdom by Baha' al-Din Zuhayr; its heading in his diwan names no occasion and no patron. It opens with longing for absent loved ones, whom he asks to pay no heed to slanderers and whose secrets he keeps, and with pride in staying true to them even when they are not, then turns to a messenger who is to carry his greeting to a beloved he will not name, encouraging him with praise and with maxims about stratagems and favours repaid. He then calls his own verse love poetry with wisdom folded inside it, and ends with that wisdom: do not waste your life, do not wait on the stars, for the matter is God's and the Law speaks true. Al-Umari and Ibn Aydamir quote from it; al-Baha' al-Amili copies the messenger lines into his al-Kashkul, and the chronicler Ibn Iyas twice cites the two lines on the stars against predictions that failed, neither naming the poet; and Ibn al-Iraqi records a line by his father on al-Isnawi's book al-Muhimmat that ends with this poem's half “it is in grave matters (muhimmat) that a man is known”. Ibn Darham, an anthologist who died in 1362 AH (1943 CE), counted it “among his finest poetry”.

translation: Pay no heed to the slanderers, what they said and what they passed on:
between me and you is something that will not come apart.
1.sharh: He asks those he loves to ignore the talebearers and everything they have invented or passed on, because what binds him to them is too strong for gossip to break. He speaks to them in the plural, as he does all through the opening.

translation: You have secrets hidden in my heart
that neither letters nor messengers can help me with.
2.sharh: His heart holds secrets that belong to them, and he has no way to get them across: no letter can hold them and no messenger carry them, because there is too much, as the next line says, and because a secret is not trusted to paper or to a go-between.

translation: The letters of longing I keep, were I to send them
to you, would not fit on all the roads and ways.
3.sharh: He has so much longing to send that, written out as letters, it would choke every road between them. The exaggeration explains the line before: what he feels is too much for any messenger to carry.

translation: Evening and morning, longing plays with me,
as if it had made me a drunken man.
4.sharh: Night and day his longing throws him about as it pleases, and he has no control over himself, like a man drunk on wine. The Arabic says he is drunk “from it”: longing itself is the wine.

translation: I take delight in a breeze from your homes,
as if its breaths, with your fragrance, were kisses.
5.sharh: A breeze that has passed over the homes of those he loves brings him their scent, and he takes each breath of it as a kiss from them. The breeze is precious because it has touched them first.

translation: How often, in my love for you, I load my heart
with what no heart could carry and endure.
6.sharh: Love for them makes him lay on his heart burdens that no heart could carry and survive, which is to say that his own heart carries them. Kam, “how many”, marks how often it happens.

translation: How often I tell it to bear your absence, and scold it,
but scolding does a lover no good.
7.sharh: He keeps urging his heart to do without them and blaming it for clinging, but blame has never cured a lover. Here the lover is both the scold and the scolded.

translation: Alas, pity a lover with so few to take his side
with you, for whom plain and mountain have grown narrow.
8.sharh: He laments over himself: no one will plead his cause with those he loves, and the whole wide earth, plains and mountains, feels too narrow to hold him. He speaks of himself as “a lover”, as if pitying a stranger.

translation: By God, my case in love is a hard one:
what to say, what to think, what to plan, what to do?
9.sharh: He swears that his case in love is a tangle he cannot find his way out of, and the second half lists his helplessness in four short questions: what to say, what to decide, how to plan, what to do. Qadiyya, “case”, is also a case at law.

translation: My verse grows lovelier when I speak of you:
love poetry is at its best about a beauty.
10.sharh: His poems improve whenever they mention the ones he loves, and he gives the reason as a general rule: love poetry is only as fine as the woman it is about. The second half reads as a proverb on its own.

translation: You who are absent, yet in my heart I see them:
whenever they part from my eyes, they are joined to me.
11.sharh: He calls out to the absent ones and then speaks of them instead: he sees them in his heart, so each parting from his eyes is a meeting inside him. The line turns on the pair infasalu, “they parted”, and ittasalu, “they were joined”.

translation: Distance has renewed their nearness in my heart,
as if the day they left were the day they came.
12.sharh: Being far from them has only brought them closer inside him, until the day they left feels like the day they arrived. The paradox finishes the thought of the line before.

translation: I am the faithful one to those I love, though they betray me;
I keep to my pledge, though they go away.
13.sharh: He boasts of his loyalty: he keeps faith with those he loves even when they break it, and holds to his promise even when they leave him. Both halves begin with ana, “I am”, and end with wa-in, “even if”.

translation: I am the lover in whose nature there is no betrayal;
far from it: my character I will not forsake.
14.sharh: Betrayal has no place in his nature, and he waves away the idea that he might change: he will never leave the character he has. The second half puts “my character” first, for weight; it can also be read “far is my character from it”, from betrayal.

translation: My messenger, then, to the one I will not name:
it is in grave matters that a man is known.
15.sharh: He turns to the messenger who will carry his words to a beloved he refuses to name, and spurs him on with a maxim: a man shows what he is worth when much is at stake.

translation: Deliver my greeting, take great care in how you speak to him,
and kiss the ground for me when you arrive.
16.sharh: The messenger is to give the beloved his greeting, choose his words with care, and kiss the ground for him on arrival. The play is between balligh, “deliver”, and baligh, “go to great lengths”.

translation: By God, tell him how I am, if you find him alone,
but do not go on: my beloved tires easily.
17.sharh: He begs the messenger to tell the beloved how he fares, but only when they are alone, and briefly, because the beloved soon grows weary. Secrecy and short words: the beloved must not be bored or exposed.

translation: This is the greatest favour I ask of you; if
you succeed, the hope I placed in you has not failed.
18.sharh: Carrying this message is the greatest thing he asks of the messenger; if he brings it off, the poet's trust in him will have been justified. The sentence runs on from the end of the first half into the second.

translation: In my affairs, whenever they arise,
I have always relied, after God, on your care.
19.sharh: He reminds the messenger of a long record: whenever something needed doing, he has relied on his care, second only to God. The praise is also encouragement for the errand in hand.

translation: In nothing you set your hand to
have you, praise God, either weakness or sloth.
20.sharh: He praises the messenger's ability and energy: whatever he takes on, he is never too weak for it nor too lazy. The words “praise God”, set in the middle of the sentence, turn the compliment into thanks.

translation: People live by people, the world pays back,
a kindness is remembered, and news travels.
21.sharh: A string of maxims to win the messenger over: people depend on one another, the world repays what is done in it, a good turn is remembered, and word of it gets around. The favour he does will not be lost.

translation: A man will find a way round when his aims are hard to reach,
and stratagems have often served those who use them.
22.sharh: When what a man wants is hard to get, he looks for a way round, and such stratagems often succeed. It may urge the messenger, praised for never failing in what he attempts, to find a way to the beloved alone; “attempt” and “stratagem” share a root in Arabic. Or the messenger is the poet's own stratagem.

translation: You for whom my words are meant: if he will listen,
he will find words that hold whatever he wishes:
23.sharh: He calls to the one his words are meant for, most likely the beloved, though it may be anyone who hears the poem, and then speaks of him as “he”: whoever listens will find in them everything he could want. The next two lines say what that is.

translation: love poetry whose tenderness steals the mind,
and in it a shining maxim or a proverb.
24.sharh: He describes his own verse: love poetry so tender it captivates, yet with a clear piece of wisdom or a proverb folded into it. It announces the turn the poem is about to take, from love to maxims.

translation: A beautiful woman needs nothing but her beauty,
the more so when she wears jewels and fine robes.
25.sharh: A beautiful woman needs no ornament, yet she is lovelier still in jewels and fine clothes; so too his love poetry, lovely in itself and lovelier for the wisdom it wears.

translation: Do not dawdle over anything you mean to do:
the turns of the nights are swift and get there first.
26.sharh: The poem turns to maxims: whatever you mean to do, do it now, because the accidents of time move fast and may get there first and put it out of reach. “The nights” stand for time and what it brings.

translation: You have wasted your life: grieve, if you have seen it;
life has no substitute and no replacement.
27.sharh: Spoken to anyone who will listen: a life frittered away is a loss to grieve over, once you see it, because nothing can be given back in its place.

translation: Race your time, for fear that it will turn:
how often have days and dynasties turned.
28.sharh: Act before time changes, because days have turned and whole states have risen and fallen with them. The same verb, “to turn”, runs through both halves.

translation: Make up your mind whenever you like, for all times are one:
neither delay nor haste wards off what is decreed.
29.sharh: There is no lucky hour to begin a thing: every hour is the same, and what God has decreed will come whether one waits or hurries. It prepares the attack on astrology that follows.

translation: Do not watch the stars over a thing you mean to do:
it is God who acts, not Capricorn or Aries.
30.sharh: Do not wait on the stars before acting, he says, because God alone makes things happen, not the signs of the zodiac. Capricorn and Aries stand for all twelve signs.

translation: Where there is good fortune, a star has no effect,
so do not let Mars or Saturn fool you.
31.sharh: When God grants good fortune, no star can change it, so do not be taken in by what astrologers say of Mars and Saturn. Good fortune is set against the two planets that astrologers held unlucky.

translation: The matter is too great, and minds are at a loss;
the Law speaks true, and man obeys.
32.sharh: The poem ends by putting fate beyond the reach of human calculation: minds can only stand bewildered before it, while the religious law tells the truth and man's part is to obey. The reciter says this last line twice.

1.1.2.head: الوُشاة
1.1.2.meaning: Wushat (singular washi): slanderers, talebearers who dress up lies, from washa, to embroider cloth.

5.2.4.head: نَشر
5.2.4.meaning: Nashr: a sweet scent, the fragrance of a person.

8.1.1-2.meaning: “Alas for pity”: a cry of lament, here over himself.

8.1.3.head: صَبّ
8.1.3.meaning: Sabb: a lover consumed by longing.

8.2.4-5.head: السَّهل وَالجَبَل
8.2.4-5.meaning: “The plain and the mountain”: the whole earth.

10.2.5.head: الغَزَل
10.2.5.meaning: Ghazal: love poetry, talk that courts a woman.

14.2.1.meaning: Hayhat: “far from it”, a word that dismisses something as out of the question.

16.2.1-2.head: قَبِّل الأَرض
16.2.1-2.meaning: “Kiss the ground”: a sign of utter respect, as people did before kings and shaykhs.

21.1.1-2.head: النّاس بِالنّاس
21.1.1-2.meaning: “People by people”: people live by one another.

21.2.2.head: ذَكَرَ
21.2.2.meaning: Is remembered, talked of. Two editions have yushkaru, “is thanked”.

24.1.2.head: خَلَبَ
24.1.2.meaning: Steals, captivates, as a woman wins a man's heart with gentle words.

24.2.3.head: غَرّاء
24.2.3.meaning: Gharra': shining, famous, as a day or a night that stands out.

25.2.1-2.meaning: La siyyama: “and above all”, “the more so”.

25.2.5.head: الحُلَل
25.2.5.meaning: Hulal (singular hulla): fine robes, a hulla being a matching wrap and mantle.

26.2.2-3.head: صَرف اللَّيالي
26.2.2-3.meaning: “The turns of the nights”: the accidents and blows of time.

27.1.5.head: فَطِنَ
27.1.5.meaning: You have noticed, realised. Some copies of the diwan have hazinta, “if you grieve for it”.

30.2.4.head: جَدي
30.2.4.meaning: Jady: Capricorn, a sign of the zodiac; the word means a kid, a young goat.

30.2.6.head: حَمَل
30.2.6.meaning: Hamal: Aries, the first sign of the zodiac; the word means a lamb.

31.2.3.head: مِرّيخ
31.2.3.meaning: Mirrikh: Mars. Astrologers called Mars and Saturn the two unlucky planets, and Jupiter and Venus the two lucky ones.

31.2.5.head: زُحَل
31.2.5.meaning: Zuhal: Saturn, which astrologers called the greater misfortune.

32.2.1.head: الشَّرع
32.2.1.meaning: Shar': the religious law that God has laid down.
